title: Choosing å or at after Norwegian verbs
goal: Choose between å-infinitives, at-clauses, and bare infinitives after common Norwegian verbs.

objectives.statement: Choose between å-infinitives, at-clauses, and bare infinitives after common Norwegian verbs.

sections.title: A weekend that depends on a deadline

spans.value: Mina and Erik are planning a weekend at a cabin. Mina is ready to leave, but Erik may have to finish some work first.
Har du bestemt deg for å bli med på hytta?

blocks.translation: Have you decided to come along to the cabin?

spans.value: Jeg håper å bli med, men sjefen sier at vi må levere rapporten på fredag.

blocks.translation: I hope to come along, but the boss says that we have to submit the report on Friday.

spans.value: Kan du jobbe med rapporten i kveld?

blocks.translation: Can you work on the report tonight?

spans.value: Ja, jeg tror at jeg kan bli ferdig før torsdag.

blocks.translation: Yes, I think that I can finish before Thursday.

spans.value: Da bør du begynne å pakke også.

blocks.translation: Then you should start packing too.

spans.value: Jeg lover at jeg skal gi deg beskjed i morgen.

blocks.translation: I promise that I will let you know tomorrow.

spans.value: The conversation contains three common ways of placing one verb or idea after another:

items.value: å followed by an infinitive: å bli, å pakke
at followed by a clause with a subject and a finite verb: at vi må levere
a bare infinitive after a modal verb: kan jobbe, bør begynne

spans.value: The choice is not simply a choice between two small words. It tells the listener how the second action or idea is connected to the first verb.
A verb complement completes the meaning of another verb. In English, compare
The infinitive (infinitiv) is the basic form of a verb, such as komme, jobbe or spise. The infinitive marker (infinitivsmerket) is å.

no.value: Erik håper å bli med.

en.value: Erik hopes to come along.

no.value: Mina planlegger å reise på fredag.

en.value: Mina plans to leave on Friday.

no.value: De prøver å bli ferdige tidlig.

en.value: They are trying to finish early.

spans.value: In these examples, the person connected to the first verb is understood as the intended or possible performer of the action in the å-infinitive. This identifies the understood subject; it does not claim that the second event actually happens:

items.value: Erik hopes, and Erik is understood as the possible person who will come.
Mina plans, and Mina is understood as the intended person who will leave.
They try, and they are understood as the intended people who may finish.

spans.value: This same-subject pattern is especially common after verbs expressing plans, wishes, attempts, beginnings and endings:

no.value: Jeg ønsker å lære mer norsk.

en.value: I want to learn more Norwegian.

no.value: Vi prøver å forstå problemet.

en.value: We are trying to understand the problem.

no.value: Hun begynner å pakke.

en.value: She begins to pack.

no.value: Han slutter å jobbe klokka fire.

en.value: He stops working at four.

no.value: De planlegger å kjøpe bil.

en.value: They are planning to buy a car.

no.value: Vi prøver å spare penger.

en.value: We are trying to save money.

spans.value: Do not give the infinitive a present-tense ending after å.

no.value: Hun prøver å komme tidlig.

en.value: She is trying to come early.

spans.value: The first verb carries the tense. The verb after å stays in the infinitive.

sections.title: When at introduces a complete clause

spans.value: The conjunction at introduces a subordinate clause (leddsetning). Unlike an å-infinitive, an at-clause normally states its own subject and contains a tense-bearing finite verb. When the finite verb is a modal, a bare infinitive may follow it.

no.value: Sjefen sier at vi må levere rapporten på fredag.

en.value: The boss says that we have to submit the report on Friday.

spans.value: The at-clause has its own subject, vi, and its finite verb is må.

no.value: Erik tror at han kan bli ferdig.

en.value: Erik thinks that he can finish.

spans.value: The at-clause has the subject han and the finite modal kan.

no.value: Mina vet at Erik jobber i kveld.

en.value: Mina knows that Erik is working tonight.

spans.value: Here the at-clause contains Erik and the present-tense verb jobber.
subject + first verb + at + subject + finite verb

no.value: Jeg tror at bussen kommer snart.

en.value: I think that the bus is coming soon.

no.value: Hun sier at møtet begynner klokka ni.

en.value: She says that the meeting begins at nine.

no.value: Vi vet at de bor i Bergen.

en.value: We know that they live in Bergen.

spans.value: Verbs of saying, thinking and knowing commonly introduce finite content clauses because what follows is a complete statement. This lesson first models the full form with

no.value: Han sier at han er sliten.

en.value: He says that he is tired.

no.value: Jeg tror at hun har tid.

en.value: I think that she has time.

no.value: De vet at toget er forsinket.

en.value: They know that the train is delayed.

spans.value: After relevant reporting and thinking verbs,
may also be omitted in natural Bokmål. For example,
remains a finite content clause with the subject
; it is not a bare infinitive.
The same-subject idea is useful, but it is not the only rule. Norwegian verbs also have their own complementation patterns. In neutral everyday Bokmål,
normally introduces a finite content clause, with or without overt

no.value: Jeg tror at jeg forstår.

en.value: I think that I understand.

no.value: Jeg tror jeg forstår.

en.value: I think that I understand.

spans.value: can occur in marked or formal Bokmål, but it is not the neutral everyday pattern practised in this lesson. None of these forms guarantees that understanding is actually achieved.
Some verbs can occur with either pattern, but the meaning relationship changes.

no.value: Jeg håper å reise på fredag.

en.value: I hope to leave on Friday.

no.value: Jeg håper at Mina reiser på fredag.

en.value: I hope that Mina leaves on Friday.

spans.value: In the first sentence, jeg is understood as the person who will leave. In the second, Mina is explicitly the person who will leave.

no.value: Erik lover å ringe i morgen.

en.value: Erik promises to call tomorrow.

no.value: Erik lover at han skal ringe i morgen.

en.value: Erik promises that he will call tomorrow.

spans.value: Both sentences can refer to Erik’s future call without guaranteeing that the call happens. The first presents Erik as the intended performer of the promised action. The second presents a complete statement about what is promised. The
-clause is useful when the subject or the whole claim needs to be explicit.

no.value: Vi håper å få svar snart.

en.value: We hope to receive an answer soon.

no.value: Vi håper at de svarer snart.

en.value: We hope that they reply soon.

spans.value: The first sentence focuses on what vi hope to experience: receiving an answer. The second states what de are hoped to do: reply.

Use the å-infinitive when the first verb naturally takes an infinitive and its subject is understood as the performer of the second action. Use an at-clause when the complement is a complete statement with its own subject and finite verb.
This is a strong working rule, but it must be combined with knowledge of the first verb. Compare:

no.value: Jeg planlegger å dra tidlig.

en.value: I plan to leave early.

no.value: Jeg tror at jeg drar tidlig.

en.value: I think that I am leaving early.

spans.value: . Norwegian similarly requires the complement pattern associated with the meaning of the first verb.
Modal verbs such as kan, skal, vil, må and bør are followed directly by a bare infinitive. A bare infinitive is an infinitive without å.

no.value: Kan du jobbe i kveld?

en.value: Can you work tonight?

no.value: Vi må levere rapporten på fredag.

en.value: We have to submit the report on Friday.

no.value: Jeg skal ringe Mina.

en.value: I will call Mina.

no.value: Erik bør begynne å pakke.

en.value: Erik should start packing.

no.value: De vil reise tidlig.

en.value: They want to leave early.

no.value: Hun kan komme.

en.value: She can come.

spans.value: After the modal, use the bare infinitive: komme.
A sentence can contain more than one complement pattern. Return to Mina’s advice:

no.value: Du bør begynne å pakke.

en.value: You should start packing.

spans.value: Here bør is a modal, so it is followed by the bare infinitive begynne. The verb begynne is then followed by an å-infinitive, å pakke.

no.value: Vi skal prøve å dra før åtte.

en.value: We will try to leave before eight.

spans.value: The bare infinitive rule applies immediately after the modal. It does not remove å from a later verb that requires an å-infinitive.

sections.title: Different written forms for different structures

spans.value: The written choice among å, at and no marker depends on grammatical structure.

no.value: Jeg prøver å forstå.

en.value: I am trying to understand.

spans.value: After prøver, the second action is an infinitive performed by the same person, so write å forstå.

no.value: Jeg tror at du forstår.

en.value: I think that you understand.

Choose the written form by examining the structure to the right:

items.value: If you need an infinitive, consider å.
If you have a subject followed by a finite verb, consider the full form with
at

at
may still introduce the same finite content clause.
If the verb immediately before the infinitive is a modal, use no marker.

no.value: Mina håper å komme.

en.value: Mina hopes to come.

no.value: Erik tror at Mina kommer.

en.value: Erik thinks that Mina is coming.

no.value: Mina kan komme.

en.value: Mina can come.

no.value: Jeg må jobbe.

en.value: I have to work.

spans.value: Modal verbs take a bare infinitive.
Using a present-tense form after å

no.value: Vi prøver å komme tidlig.

en.value: We are trying to come early.

spans.value: The verb after å stays in the infinitive.
Omitting the subject from an at-clause
Mina sier at kommer på fredag.

no.value: Mina sier at hun kommer på fredag.

en.value: Mina says that she is coming on Friday.

spans.value: An at-clause normally needs its own subject.
Marked or formal Bokmål can use
, but the neutral everyday pattern practised here is a finite content clause:

no.value: Jeg tror at jeg rekker bussen.

en.value: I think that I will catch the bus.

no.value: Jeg tror jeg rekker bussen.

en.value: I think that I will catch the bus.

The next morning, Mina receives a message.
Sjefen sier at rapporten er godkjent.

blocks.translation: The boss says that the report has been approved.

spans.value: Betyr det at du kan bli med?

blocks.translation: Does that mean that you can come along?

spans.value: Ja. Jeg skal prøve å gå fra kontoret klokka tre.

blocks.translation: Yes. I will try to leave the office at three.

spans.value: Fint! Jeg håper å kjøre før rushtiden begynner.

blocks.translation: Great! I hope to drive before rush hour begins.

spans.value: Jeg tror at jeg rekker det.

blocks.translation: I think that I can make it.

spans.value: The forms now work together naturally:

items.value: sier at introduces a complete statement
kan bli uses a bare infinitive after a modal
skal prøve uses a bare infinitive after a modal
prøve å gå uses an å-infinitive
håper å kjøre presents Mina’s own hoped-for action
tror at introduces Erik’s complete thought

sections.title: Transfer: A change of everyday situation

spans.value: Now move from a cabin trip to a shared dinner. Nora is cooking for friends, but Jonas is delayed at work.
A complete account might need several kinds of meaning:

items.value: what Jonas says about his delay
what Nora plans to prepare
what the guests can bring
what Nora thinks will happen
what Jonas will try to do

spans.value: Use these questions when choosing a complement:

items.value: Does the first verb take an action infinitive, often performed by the same person? Use
å + infinitive
Does the first verb introduce a complete statement with its own subject and finite verb? Use a finite content clause. The full form has
at
; relevant reporting and thinking verbs may allow
at
to be omitted.
Is the infinitive immediately after a modal such as kan, skal, vil, må or bør? Use a
bare infinitive

prompt.value: Read this cabin exchange: Mina asks «Har du bestemt deg for å bli med på hytta?» Erik replies «Jeg håper å bli med, men sjefen sier at vi må levere rapporten på fredag.» Mina asks «Kan du jobbe med rapporten i kveld?» Erik says «Ja, jeg tror at jeg kan bli ferdig før torsdag.» Mina says «Da bør du begynne å pakke også.» Erik promises «Jeg lover at jeg skal gi deg beskjed i morgen.» Choose the complete reading. Identify who performs each action and which complement contains another explicitly stated subject.

options.text: Mina is expected to come, Mina submits the report, Mina works tonight, Mina packs, and Mina gives the answer; all actions have the same understood subject.
options.why: The exchange addresses Erik as du and jeg, and the report clause explicitly states vi.

options.text: Erik comes, Erik alone submits the report, Erik works, Erik packs, and Mina gives the answer; the at-clause has no separate subject.
options.why: The report clause has the explicit subject vi, and the final clause has the explicit subject jeg.

options.text: «Har du bestemt deg for å bli med på hytta?» — Erik is the person expected to come; «Jeg håper å bli med» — Erik hopes to come; «sjefen sier at vi må levere rapporten på fredag» — vi is the stated subject that has to submit; «Kan du jobbe med rapporten i kveld?» — Erik can work tonight; «Da bør du begynne å pakke også» — Erik should pack; «Jeg lover at jeg skal gi deg beskjed i morgen» — Erik is the person who will give the answer. The report action has another explicitly stated subject, vi.
options.why: The å-actions are understood as Erik’s actions, while the at-clause about submitting explicitly states vi as its subject.

prompt.value: Classify every statement by identifying whether the person connected to the first verb is the intended or possible performer, and mark which statements use an å-infinitive for that relationship.

options.text: All four statements use an å-infinitive, and the first-verb subject performs every second action.
options.why: The last two statements use at-clauses, and the third explicitly names Mina inside its clause.

options.text: «Erik håper å bli med.» — Erik is the understood performer, and this is the å-infinitive relationship. «Mina planlegger å reise på fredag.» — Mina is the understood performer, and this is the å-infinitive relationship. «Jeg håper at Mina reiser på fredag.» — Mina is explicitly stated in an at-clause, not an å-infinitive. «Jeg tror at jeg forstår.» — this is a finite at-clause, not an å-infinitive.
options.why: The å-infinitive examples link the second action to the person connected to the first verb; the at-clauses state their own finite clause structure.

options.text: The first two statements use å-infinitives, but «Jeg håper at Mina reiser på fredag.» also uses an å-infinitive because Mina is the performer.
options.why: A stated subject and finite verb after at form a complete clause, not an å-infinitive.

options.text: «Jeg håper å reise på fredag.» — I hope to leave on Friday. «Jeg håper at Mina reiser på fredag.» — I hope that Mina leaves on Friday. «Jeg tror at jeg drar tidlig.» — I think that I am leaving early.
